Great question! Here's a simple rule of thumb:

Use useState when:

  • You have simple, independent state values
  • State updates are straightforward

Use useReducer when:

  • You have multiple related state values
  • Next state depends on previous state
  • You have complex update logic

Think of useReducer as useState's bigger sibling for complex scenarios.

A shopping cart, good example it is!

With useState, track items, quantities, totals separately you must. Messy it becomes.

With useReducer, actions like ADD_ITEM, REMOVE_ITEM, UPDATE_QUANTITY you dispatch. Cleaner the code stays.

Let me walk through it:

The recurrence relation is: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)

This forms a binary tree where each node spawns 2 children. The height is n, so roughly 2^n nodes.

More precisely, T(n) ≈ φ^n where φ (golden ratio) ≈ 1.618

So O(2^n) is a simplification, but captures the exponential nature.

I found drawing the recursion tree helpful!

For fib(5), you calculate fib(4) and fib(3). But then fib(4) also calculates fib(3)... so you're repeating work!

That's why memoization or bottom-up DP makes it O(n) instead.

BFS:

  • Shortest path in unweighted graphs
  • Level-order traversal
  • Finding nodes within k distance

DFS:

  • Detecting cycles
  • Topological sorting
  • Finding connected components
  • Maze solving

Memory-wise: BFS uses more memory (stores entire level), DFS is more space-efficient for deep graphs.

Consider a table: Student(student_id, name, dept_id, dept_name)

Transitive dependency: student_id → dept_id → dept_name

Here, dept_name depends on dept_id, not directly on student_id. To achieve 3NF, split into:

  • Student(student_id, name, dept_id)
  • Department(dept_id, dept_name)

For 192.168.1.0/24:

Usable hosts: 2^(32-24) - 2 = 254 hosts

(We subtract 2 for network address and broadcast)

Broadcast address: 192.168.1.255

The /24 means first 24 bits are network, last 8 bits for hosts. All 1s in host portion = broadcast.

Try wrapping your route config in useMemo or using a component-based approach instead of inline functions.

Here's a clean pattern I recommend:

const ProtectedRoute = ({ children }) => {
  const { user } = useAuth();
  return user ? children : <Navigate to="/login" />;
};

Then wrap your protected routes with this component. No infinite loops!

Create custom hooks when you find yourself:

  1. Repeating the same logic across multiple components
  2. Combining multiple built-in hooks for a specific purpose
  3. Wanting to abstract away complex state logic

Reusability is the main criterion. If it's only used once, keep it in the component.

React.memo is great for preventing re-renders when props haven't changed.

useMemo is for expensive calculations within a component.

try {

Then conditionally render error UI based on that state.

Classic overfitting, this is!

More solutions, try you should:

  • Early stopping - stop training when validation accuracy plateaus
  • Reduce model complexity - fewer layers or neurons
  • More training data - augmentation helps
  • L2 regularization in addition to dropout
  • Batch normalization

Start with early stopping first!

With 10,000 images, you have enough data to unfreeze more layers.

I'd suggest:

  1. Start by freezing all but last layer, train for 5-10 epochs
  2. Unfreeze last 2-3 conv blocks, reduce learning rate by 10x
  3. Train until convergence

This "progressive unfreezing" works well in practice.

The attention mechanism is actually quite elegant once you get it!

Think of it like a database lookup:

  • Query: "What am I looking for?"
  • Key: "What do I contain?"
  • Value: "What information do I store?"

Self-attention compares each word's query to all keys, then retrieves weighted values. This lets the model focus on relevant parts of the input.

Batch size is a trade-off between:

  • Memory: Larger batches need more GPU memory
  • Gradient quality: Smaller batches are noisier but can escape local minima
  • Training speed: Larger batches train faster per epoch

Try 32 or 64 as a starting point. If you have GPU memory, 64 is usually a good balance.

Here's a comparison:

ReduceLROnPlateau: Safest option - reduces LR when validation loss plateaus. Set patience=5-10 epochs.

Cosine annealing: Smooth decay, good for longer training.

Step decay: Simple, drops LR at fixed intervals.

I'd start with ReduceLROnPlateau since it adapts to your specific training dynamics.

For missing values, the approach depends on:

  1. If data is MCAR (Missing Completely At Random): Dropping rows is okay
  2. If missing values have patterns: Use imputation

With 20% missing, I'd use imputation. Start with median for numerical features and mode for categorical.

Libraries like sklearn's SimpleImputer or fancyimpute can help!

Choose BST when you need:

  • Sorted order iteration
  • Range queries (find all elements between x and y)
  • Order statistics (find kth smallest)

Choose Hash Table when:

  • You only need exact lookups
  • Order doesn't matter
  • You want O(1) average case vs O(log n) for BST

Hash tables are generally faster but BSTs are more versatile.

A* is better when you have a good heuristic function and want to reach a specific goal node.

For the heuristic, use:

  • Euclidean distance for grid-based pathfinding
  • Manhattan distance if you can only move in 4 directions

The key: heuristic must be admissible (never overestimate actual cost) for A* to guarantee shortest path.

Dijkstra is just A* with heuristic = 0.

I am Groot! (Translation: Proving greedy algorithms requires two steps)

  1. Greedy choice property: Show local optimal choice leads to global optimum
  2. Optimal substructure: Optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems

I am Groot! (Use proof by contradiction - assume greedy doesn't work, then show this leads to a contradiction)

However, for small datasets on modern machines, prioritize code clarity over micro-optimizations.

The allocation matrix is determined by the current state of the system - which resources are currently held by which processes.

In practice, the OS maintains this through resource allocation tables. When a process requests resources, the system checks if granting it would leave the system in a safe state using Banker's algorithm.

For your lab, you'll be given the initial allocation - focus on implementing the safety algorithm!

Good question! The optimal quantum depends on your context switch overhead.

General guidelines:

  • Too small (< 10ms): High overhead from context switching
  • Too large (> 100ms): Poor responsiveness
  • Sweet spot: 20-50ms for interactive systems

Rule of thumb: quantum should be ~10x the context switch time.

Large pages reduce page table overhead but cause internal fragmentation.

With 4MB pages:

  • If a process only needs 100KB, you waste 3.9MB
  • Fewer page faults, but more wasted memory
  • Worse memory utilization

4KB is the standard compromise. Some systems offer "huge pages" (2MB) as an optimization for specific workloads like databases.

Excellent question! Counting semaphores are perfect for:

  1. Resource pools: Limited number of identical resources (e.g., 5 database connections)
  2. Producer-consumer: Buffer with finite capacity
  3. Rate limiting: Allow max N concurrent operations

Example: Parking lot with 100 spaces. Semaphore initialized to 100. Each car entering does wait(), leaving does signal().

Mutex is just a semaphore with count=1, specialized for mutual exclusion.

I'd go with RAID 10 if you can afford it! Here's why:

RAID 5:

  • Better storage efficiency (n-1 drives usable)
  • Slower writes (parity calculation)
  • Vulnerable during rebuild

RAID 10:

  • Excellent performance (no parity overhead)
  • Better reliability
  • 50% storage efficiency

For a database, RAID 10 is worth the extra cost!

Your query is missing indexes! Add these:

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders(date);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_product ON orders(product_id);

Also, use SELECT specific columns instead of SELECT *. You're pulling unnecessary data.

After adding indexes, check the execution plan with EXPLAIN to verify they're being used.

READ_COMMITTED: Sees only committed data, but data can change during transaction (non-repeatable reads possible)

REPEATABLE_READ: Once you read data, it won't change until transaction ends (prevents non-repeatable reads)

Choose READ_COMMITTED for better concurrency when you can tolerate minor inconsistencies.

Use REPEATABLE_READ for financial transactions or when consistency is critical.

Performance: READ_COMMITTED is faster due to less locking.

Use PostgreSQL when:

Connection pooling best practices from my experience:

Formula: pool_size = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)

For your case with ~1000 req/min:

  • Start with pool size of 20-30
  • Monitor connection usage
  • Adjust based on actual utilization
  • Set max_connections on PostgreSQL to pool_size * num_app_servers

More connections ≠ better performance. Too many causes context switching overhead!

I had this exact issue! Check:

  1. Phase 1 IKE negotiation: Are encryption algorithms matching on both sides?
  2. Authentication: Pre-shared keys must be identical
  3. DPD (Dead Peer Detection): Timeout settings might be too aggressive
  4. NAT-T: If behind NAT, ensure NAT-T is enabled

Use packet capture on both sides to see where negotiation fails. Wireshark can decode IKE packets!

Router-on-a-stick uses one physical interface with subinterfaces (802.1Q trunking). Cheaper but slower - traffic must traverse router.

Layer 3 switch routes at wire speed in hardware. Much faster, but more expensive.

For 3 VLANs with moderate traffic, router-on-a-stick is fine. For production with heavy inter-VLAN traffic, invest in L3 switch.

Think of TCP congestion control as driving on a highway:

Slow Start: You just merged - accelerate quickly (exponential growth) until you reach speed limit or sense congestion

Congestion Avoidance: Cruising at highway speed - increase slowly (linear growth), careful not to cause traffic jam

Switch happens at ssthresh (slow start threshold). After packet loss, ssthresh is updated and you restart slow start.

Quick DNS record guide:

A record: Maps domain to IPv4 address
example.com → 192.0.2.1

AAAA record: Maps domain to IPv6 address
example.com → 2001:0db8::1

CNAME: Alias to another domain
www.example.com → example.com

Use CNAME for aliases (www, blog, etc). Use A/AAAA for root domain and direct IP mapping. Can't use CNAME for root domain!

This is a common issue - HTTP runs on TCP port 80/443, ping uses ICMP (different protocol).

Possibilities:

  1. Firewall blocking HTTP: Allows ICMP but blocks TCP 80/443
  2. Web server not running: OS responds to ping but no HTTP service
  3. SELinux/AppArmor: Security policy blocking web server

Test with: telnet server_ip 80 or curl -v http://server_ip

Check firewall: iptables -L or firewall-cmd --list-all

The "5 users find 85% of issues" comes from Jakob Nielsen's research.

For your project:

  • Minimum: 5 participants (as stated in requirements)
  • Ideal: 8-10 for more confidence

Participants should match your target demographic as closely as possible. Recruiting the wrong users can lead to misleading results.

Focus on qualitative insights rather than statistical significance - HCI is about understanding user behavior, not just numbers!

For WCAG 2.1 AA compliance:

  • Normal text: 4.5:1 minimum contrast ratio
  • Large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold): 3:1 minimum
  • Logos and decorative elements: No contrast requirements
  • UI components (buttons, form fields): 3:1 minimum

Use tools like WebAIM Contrast Checker or Chrome DevTools to test. They'll tell you if you pass AA standards!

To avoid leading questions, use the "How might we..." framework:

Bad (leading): "Don't you think the checkout process is too complicated?"

Good (open-ended): "Walk me through your last online purchase. What was that experience like?"

Tips:

  • Ask "why" to dig deeper
  • Use silence - let them think
  • Focus on behaviors, not opinions
  • "Tell me about a time when..."

Dude, for A/B testing you need to calculate sample size based on:

  1. Baseline conversion: 5%
  2. Minimum detectable effect: How much improvement matters? (e.g., 0.5%)
  3. Statistical power: Usually 80%
  4. Significance level: Usually 5% (α = 0.05)

Use online calculators like Optimizely or Evan Miller's. For 5% baseline with 20% relative lift, you'd need ~4000 users per variant.

Don't stop early - let it run to calculated sample size!

The issue is that depends_on only waits for container to START, not be READY.

Solutions:

  1. Use wait-for-it script:
    command: ["/wait-for-it.sh", "db:5432", "--", "npm", "start"]
  2. Add healthcheck to DB:
    healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD", "pg_isready"]
  interval: 5s
  3. Use restart policy:
    restart: on-failure

I recommend option 2 - proper healthchecks make your stack more robust!

I evaluated both for my project. Here's the breakdown:

Use Lambda when:

  • Sporadic, event-driven workload ✓ (fits your case!)
  • Stateless operations
  • Want zero infrastructure management
  • Can tolerate cold starts

Use EC2 when:

  • Constant high traffic
  • Need specific OS/runtime control
  • Long-running processes

For sporadic traffic with spikes, Lambda is perfect. You only pay for execution time. With EC2, you pay 24/7 even during idle periods.

For your requirements, I'd suggest GitHub Actions:

GitHub Actions Pros:

  • Native GitHub integration
  • Free for public repos, generous for private
  • Simple YAML config
  • AWS deployment via official actions
  • Less maintenance overhead

Jenkins Pros:

  • More powerful and flexible
  • Better for complex pipelines
  • Self-hosted = more control

Since you're already on GitHub and need simple AWS deployment, GitHub Actions is the easier choice. You can always migrate to Jenkins later if needed.

Terraform is better for multi-cloud!

Here's why we chose Terraform:

  • Cloud-agnostic: Same language for AWS, Azure, GCP
  • State management: Track infrastructure changes
  • Larger ecosystem: More modules and providers
  • Better for version control: Infrastructure as code

CloudFormation is AWS-only. If you might switch to Azure, you'd have to rewrite everything. With Terraform, just swap providers!

Plus, Terraform has better tooling (terraform plan is amazing for previewing changes).

Container security is critical! Here are free tools you should integrate:

  1. Trivy: Excellent, easy to use
    trivy image your-image:tag
  2. Grype: From Anchore, good vulnerability detection
  3. Docker Scout: Built into Docker Desktop
  4. Snyk: Free for open source

For CI/CD integration, add to GitHub Actions:

- name: Run Trivy
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: 'your-image:tag'

Fail the build if high/critical vulnerabilities are found!
